title: A piece of broiled fish (Luke 24:36–49)
hookLine: he's no ghost: touch me, see my hands, give me something to eat

lines: BACK FROM EMMAUS, OUT OF BREATH.
cards: The two from Emmaus have just burst back into the room in Jerusalem. The others tell them, the Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon. And the two tell their story of the road and the bread.

While they're still talking, Jesus himself is standing in the middle of them. He says, in the King James words, "Peace be unto you." And everyone in the room, people who just said they believed, is terrified.
Luke says they thought they were seeing a spirit. A ghost. Which is exactly what anyone would think.

teach.b: Jesus asks why they're troubled, and then he does something very physical. "Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have." Handle me.
Then a line that sounds like a real room full of people: "And while they yet believed not for joy, and wondered." They can't believe it, not from doubt, but because it's too good.

And Jesus answers with the most ordinary question in the world: "Have ye here any meat?" Meat meant food of any kind. They give him a piece of broiled fish, and he takes it and eats it in front of them.
Christian writers from the second century on made a lot of this small scene. The risen Jesus isn't a vision or a memory or an idea. He has hands with wounds in them.
He eats what's on the table. Christians teach that the resurrection is of the body, and Luke wants you to see a body.

Then he opens their understanding of the scriptures and gives them a job: to preach repentance and forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things, he says.

teach.h: YOU ARE WITNESSES; WAIT FOR POWER.
teach.b: But first, wait in the city until you're clothed with power from on high.

teach.h: A SPIRIT HATH NOT FLESH AND BONES.
teach.b: That next chapter is Luke's second book, Acts. Today's is smaller: a frightened room, wounded hands, and a piece of fish.

how: Christians confess in the ancient creeds belief in the resurrection of the body, and many churches read this appearance in the weeks after Easter.

the soul's flight from the body at death

games.q: you're risen, standing among your terrified friends, who think you're a ghost. how do you show them?
o: show your hands and feet, and ask for something to eat.
tell them to have more faith.
games.why: "handle me, and see"; then, "have ye here any meat?" he eats a piece of broiled fish before them.

practice: If you have something small to eat nearby, a piece of fruit, a cracker, look at it first, its color and weight, then eat it slowly, the way you'd eat in front of someone you hadn't seen in a long time.
Let yourself be glad, simply, that you have a body, and food, and this minute; if there's no food near you, just notice your hands and feet. If you pray, you can give thanks before you eat.

wordCard.voice: Resurrection. What the risen Jesus proved to his frightened friends by showing his wounded hands and eating a piece of broiled fish in front of them.

orig.note: Greek: touch, handle, feel with your hands. the word behind 'handle me, and see'.

carryVoice: Your line: handle me and see. Not a ghost: hands, feet, and a meal. See you tomorrow.
